Femicide

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
SA holds the highest Femicide rate in the world - five times higher than the rate globally. They're almost always all beautiful and young, why are they being killed?

Summary:
SA holds the highest Femicide rate in the world - five times higher than the rate globally. They're almost always all beautiful and young, why are they being killed?

Intimate Femicide - the killing of a female by an intimate partner (husband, boyfriend, life partner) is considered to be the most extreme form and consequence of intimate partner violence. It is the leading cause of death for female murder victims in South Africa. A woman is killed by her intimate partner every eight hours in South Africa - three women a day. Globally, more than 35% of all murders of women are reported to be committed by an intimate partner.

Further information:
In comparison, 5% of all murders on men are committed by an intimate partner.
Evidence also shows that when women kill their intimate partners, it is mostly done in self-defence following ongoing violence and intimidation.

When we hear of a women who was murdered, what jumps to mind first is whether her husband or boyfriend of life partner was involved. Why? In South Africa we have had a litany of high-profile cases that have been characterized in this way.

The most obvious example is Oscar Pistorius shooting his model-girlfriend in the early hours of Valentine's Day in 2013 in his house in Pretoria. He was found guilty on culpable homicide, sentenced to five years in prison, and will be released on correctional supervision on 21 August this year after serving once sixth of his prison term. The NPA is appealing Judge Masipa's verdict in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein in November, asking that it be overturned to a guilty conviction on murder.

Shrien Dewani, the so-called honeymoon murder accused, stood trial for arrnaging a hit on his wife, Anni in Gugulethu in November 2012. Three men were arrested in connection with the murder and they claimed Dewani offered them money to kill Anni, but he was aquitted.

Nico Henning, allegedly the mastermind behind the killing of his estranged wife, Chanelle Henning in November 2011, will stand trial in October. Chanelle was gunned down in Faerie Glen just after dropping her son off at school.

Tato Kutumela was convicted and sentenced ten years for raping and 20 years for killing his 18-year old model girlfriend, Zanele Khumalo in April 2011. He raped her, strangled her and covered her naked body with a blanket in her parents house in Pretoria, before he dressed and left for work. At the same time that Oscar Pistorius stood trial, Tato Kutumela was in the court next door was days in March last year, for proceedings in mitigation of his 20-year jail sentence.

Dieter Bergs, 79, was charged in September last year for the murder of his wife of 10 years, Genee Bergs, national publicity manager of Estee Lauder. She was shot through the chest twice in March last year and at first Bergs claimed it was a robbery and that he had also injured his hip. Bergs is well-known in social circles in Johannesburg and had also served on the board of the Johannesburg Philharmonic Orchestra. He was arrested in September last years and released on bail of R10 000.

Rameez Patel has been released on bail last month in Polokwane for the murder of his wife. At first Patel also claimed there was a burglary.

Christopher Panayioytou has been denied bail and is being held in custody in Port Elizabeth for the alleged murder on his young wife, Jayde. She disappeared and a day later her body was found on the outskirts of Uitenhage in the Eastern Cape. A love triangle is being put forward by the state as a possible motive for the murder.

Press Release:


Intimate Femicide
Four months before Zanele Khumalo died, she wrote in her diary: “...today is the last day a man abuses me.” Little did she know she would be strangled to death by her boyfriend and father of her unborn child. With a death every eight hours, South Africa has a femicide rate five times higher than the global average. Carte Blanche investigates a handful of compelling intimate femicide cases that beg the question - what will it take to bring down levels of violence against women?


Script:


FEMICIDE SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

THEMBA: Her mother shook her, she wasn’t responding, I became suspicious, I joined in shaking her, then we discovered the truth about her, she was lying there dead

SHARON: I always think that Chanelle could have still been here, but somebody else wanted to play God.

FAROOK CHOONARA: It brings anger in a person, a lot of anger, to think that a young, lively, vibrant person could be murdered in such a brutal manner.

Chanelle Henning: murdered in 2011 outside her toddler’s school in Pretoria;
Zanele Khumalo: raped and strangled in her parents house in Pretoria in 2011;
Jayde Panayiotou: abducted outside her house and shot in the Eastern Cape in April;
Fatima Patel: severely assaulted and shot at her house in Polokwane in April.

All had a lover accused of having a hand in their deaths.

LISA VETTEN: Many of these high-profile cases had often attracted attention, because they are exceptional, not because they are the norm.

Gender activist, Lisa Vetten says the norm is in fact that every day, ordinary unknown women are killed by their ordinary unknown intimate partners. But these killings aren’t always sensational enough to make headlines.

LISA VETTEN: Focusing on the high-profile cases should actually make us stop and pause and think, who are the women whose cases we are not focusing on? Our statistics say that three women every day die at the hands of their intimate partners.

That is every eight hours…
South Africa has a femicide rate five times higher than the global average.

ANNI HESSELINK: Research proves and it illustrates that the chances of woman murdered by someone that she knows and someone in an intimate relationship is much higher than any other murder.

Criminologist Anni Hesselink has been working in South African prisons for the past twenty-two years and says our high intimate femicide rate reflects our tolerance of violence.

ANNI HESSELINK: It is a reflection of the ill society that we live in, of the social fabric that we have, of the normlessness. I often say I think I am safer in prison than what I am in society, because at least in prison I know who are there and why they are there for, whereas in society, your nextdoor neighbor who seems like the normal guy next door, is often a serial killer, is often the wife abuser, is often the paedophile and the child abuser.

LISA VETTEN: Why is it that we only pay attention if the person is famous or if the killing is extremely unusual, exotic and bizarre and in the end do we not do an injustice by ignoring all those other deaths.

Lesser known cases include 18-year old Zanele Khumalo - raped and strangled by her boyfriend, Thato Kutumelo in April 2011.
In March last year, Kutumelo was sentenced to an effective twenty years in the courtroom adjacent to that in which Oscar Pistorius was standing trial.

THEMBA KHUMALO: I can’t say we have forgiven him, justice has been done, he is serving a prison sentence, but we will not forget what he did to us.

Zanele’s father, Themba, says she introduced Thato to her family eleven months before she died.

THEMBA: Around the festive season in 2010, we went out as a family on holiday and Zanele didn’t behave, you know, like the usual Zanele, the usual daughter, the bubbly, outgoing, happy child. We could see there is something she is hiding. On hindsight we found that it is when the beating, the physical abuse started, when this guy physically started abusing her.

At the time of her death she was five months pregnant and had ended the relationship, accepting she would raise her child as a single mother.

Unbeknown to her family, four months before her death she wrote in her diary: “I know I have messed up for twelve months and now I have to face the consequences of my actions. I am starting my life without you and writing that on its own, is “reliefing”. Today is the last day any man abuses me (mentally, emotionally, physically). I have bruises on my body and the smile on your face after hurting me, shows how sick you are. God, please send me a miracle.”

THEMBA: About a month before her death I came home from work, I found her crying and she just volunteered the information that she had been assaulted by her boyfriend. He tried to strangle her right in the house. I asked him not to set his foot here again. He agreed and he left.

But Themba says Thato continued threatening and contacting Zanele.
A month later, he raped and strangled her at her parents house.

BONGANI: How big a role does sexual jealousy play?

LISA VETTEN: It is probably the leading precipitating factor. You are mine, and if you leave me, I am not going to be able to tolerate that kind of insult to my ego.

LEONARD CARR: The key element that is a common dominator is that in the killing of another there is the objectification of the other – the other becomes merely an object of your gratification when that person no longer serves you or serves your interests, then it is more convenient to just get rid of them, dispose of them, you do that.

Clinical psychologist, Leonard Carr even goes so far as to call intimate femicide a form of divorce.

LEONARD CARR: It has become a highly practised form of divorce, because particularly in this country where there is so much hijacking, I have clients who are petrified because they know that their partners hare taken hits on them, so with hijacking it is certainly a way to dispose of someone without anybody being any wiser.

Fatima Patel was murdered in April in her house in Polokwane. Her family is still in shock says her uncle, Farook Choonara.

BONGANI: Did anyone in the family see this coming?

FAROOK CHOOKARA: No, we all thought they were a happy couple. You know, we all want to find how did this… what happened, how did this thing take place.

Fatima’s husband, Rameez was arrested less than a week after she died and released on bail of R250 000. He has not yet pleaded to the charge, but maintains he’s innocence, claiming robbers killed his wife. The case continues.

FAROOK CHOONARA: The family want justice. Her skull was cracked, her cheekbones were broken, her jaw was dislodged, on top of all, she was still shot in her face.

Anni says common themes run through most intimate femicide killings.

ANNI: The motives here often are for financial reasons, adultery or a love-triangle and or whether there is a custody or a residential battle for children –

Two hitmen were allegedly paid by Jayde Panayioutou’s husband, Christopher. Jayde was murdered after being kidnapped outside their house in Port Elizabeth in April. Her body was found on the outskirts of KwaNobuhle, outside Uitenhage. Panayioutou was arrested and charged with conspiracy to commit murder and defeating the ends of justice.
He indicated he would plead not guilty. He was denied bail, but is appealing this ruling.

Hitmen were also used to kill Chanelle Henning. Her parents, Sharon and Ivan believe a custody battle between their daughter and her estranged husband, Nico Henning was motive for her murder.

Her two killers pleaded guilty and are serving 18-year sentences.
Nico’s best friend, Andre Gouws and former Nigerian Olympic athlete, Ambrose Monye, confessed to being involved after they were convicted and are both serving life-sentences.
Nico was arrested in December 2013 after Gouws testified he had offered him a million rand to have his wife killed. The trial starts on the 5th of October and he has not yet pleaded to the charges of murder and conspiracy to murder.

BONGANI: Was it ever your sense that Nico could be a dangerous person?

Ivan: Everything about him was just in place. He used to treat her well, he used to spoil her well, he used to respect us.

BONGANI: How long did the good times last?

Sharon: When they got back from honeymoon, she told us, that was the biggest mistake she made, because the day they got married, he changed and he was totally a different person. He became very abusive, not physically, but breaking her down every chance he got.

LEONARD CARR: No abuser ever knocks on your door for a date and says: “Good evening, nice to meet you, do you want to enter into an abusive relationship with me?” Rather it starts out very charming and then the negative behaviour will be subtle, it will be a look, a remark, that makes the other person feel upset or put down. But then it will be followed by charm. So what you see is that abusers always switch

BONGANI: Why did Chanelle stay?

Sharon: Well, she didn’t. She tried to leave him a few times. She left him twice and he begged her everytime to come back

LISA VETTEN: There may be threats that if you leave, I can’t live without you. And that might sound very flattering that someone loves you so much that they would rather die, but it is actually very dangerous.

BONGANI LINK: The statistics around intimate femicide are truly shocking. This problem is a lot more prevalent than many of us are comfortable to believe. So, how are we all playing a part in aiding it?

Most people avoid get involved in a neighbour’s or family member’s domestic disputes.

LISA VETTEN: What has happened in people’s homes, is none of our business, we don’t get involved. They must sort it out between the two of them.

BONGANI LINK: There is no doubt that the SA police service is under pressure to deal with very violent crimes. But how sensitized is the average officer to deal with intimate femicide?

LISA VETTEN: Unfortunately, we know have for example four cases that have been brought against the police, two successful so far, two are still being heard, that have pointed to police negligence and the police had to pay damages. They had resulted in police failing to act on violence and resulted in women being raped or murdered. In 2009, 55 of the women who were killed in that year by their intimate partners, had protection orders at the time.

THEMBA: Had I known the seriousness of the situation as a father, I would have done something. My daughter would be alive today had she had been open with us.

SHARON: A year before she was murdered, we actually said to them at court, the legal team, if you guys do not do something now to protect her, he is going to have her killed and they told me in court that I am paranoid. Three weeks before she was murdered she asked us to promise her that if anything happens to her, we would fight for her son and that is what we did.

Chanelle and Nico’s son was four when his mother was gunned down. He was placed in foster care for eight months after her death, while Ivan and Sharon fought for custody.

Sharon: we had to undergo evaluations to make sure we are normal and can take care of him and that is something that I can’t get over, because you have lost your daughter, your grandson that has been living with you for 18 months gets ripped away from you, because of a system. Benjamin should have been with us, not with strangers.

The custody battle is ongoing and Nico has unsupervised visits every second weekend.

BONGANI LINK: At the core of public support for the court system, is not only the idea that justice is done, but that justice is seen to be done. This however, is threatened when people believe that perpetrators are given lenient sentences.

Henning, Patel and Panayioutou will face their day in court. Kutumelo is currently serving a 20 year sentence and will remain behind bars for at least three-quarters of this term.

THEMBA: I don’t know whether the sentences that the culprits are given in court are not deterrent enough. It is painful for us parents to have gone through this.

FAROOK: If you have a problem with a person, why can’t you come to an amicable settlement, each one go their way, why do you have to murder a person?

SHARON: It is time our system and our country take this kind of killing very serious, because this is not right. Our daughters and our grandchildren’s mothers shouldn’t be killed for any reason.

Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 31 August 2015 Press Release: Intimate Femicide Four months before Zanele Khumalo died, she wrote in her diary: “...today is the last day a man abuses me.” Little did she know she would be strangled to death by her boyfriend and father of her unborn child. With a death every eight hours, South Africa has a femicide rate five times higher than the global average. Carte Blanche investigates a handful of compelling intimate femicide cases that beg the question - what will it take to bring down levels of violence against women? Script: FEMICIDE SCRIPT PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK THEMBA: Her mother shook her, she wasn’t responding, I became suspicious, I joined in shaking her, then we discovered the truth about her, she was lying there dead SHARON: I always think that Chanelle could have still been here, but somebody else wanted to play God. FAROOK CHOONARA: It brings anger in a person, a lot of anger, to think that a young, lively, vibrant person could be murdered in such a brutal manner. Chanelle Henning: murdered in 2011 outside her toddler’s school in Pretoria; Zanele Khumalo: raped and strangled in her parents house in Pretoria in 2011; Jayde Panayiotou: abducted outside her house and shot in the Eastern Cape in April; Fatima Patel: severely assaulted and shot at her house in Polokwane in April. All had a lover accused of having a hand in their deaths. LISA VETTEN: Many of these high-profile cases had often attracted attention, because they are exceptional, not because they are the norm. Gender activist, Lisa Vetten says the norm is in fact that every day, ordinary unknown women are killed by their ordinary unknown intimate partners. But these killings aren’t always sensational enough to make headlines. LISA VETTEN: Focusing on the high-profile cases should actually make us stop and pause and think, who are the women whose cases we are not focusing on? Our statistics say that three women every day die at the hands of their intimate partners. That is every eight hours… South Africa has a femicide rate five times higher than the global average. ANNI HESSELINK: Research proves and it illustrates that the chances of woman murdered by someone that she knows and someone in an intimate relationship is much higher than any other murder. Criminologist Anni Hesselink has been working in South African prisons for the past twenty-two years and says our high intimate femicide rate reflects our tolerance of violence. ANNI HESSELINK: It is a reflection of the ill society that we live in, of the social fabric that we have, of the normlessness. I often say I think I am safer in prison than what I am in society, because at least in prison I know who are there and why they are there for, whereas in society, your nextdoor neighbor who seems like the normal guy next door, is often a serial killer, is often the wife abuser, is often the paedophile and the child abuser. LISA VETTEN: Why is it that we only pay attention if the person is famous or if the killing is extremely unusual, exotic and bizarre and in the end do we not do an injustice by ignoring all those other deaths. Lesser known cases include 18-year old Zanele Khumalo - raped and strangled by her boyfriend, Thato Kutumelo in April 2011. In March last year, Kutumelo was sentenced to an effective twenty years in the courtroom adjacent to that in which Oscar Pistorius was standing trial. THEMBA KHUMALO: I can’t say we have forgiven him, justice has been done, he is serving a prison sentence, but we will not forget what he did to us. Zanele’s father, Themba, says she introduced Thato to her family eleven months before she died. THEMBA: Around the festive season in 2010, we went out as a family on holiday and Zanele didn’t behave, you know, like the usual Zanele, the usual daughter, the bubbly, outgoing, happy child. We could see there is something she is hiding. On hindsight we found that it is when the beating, the physical abuse started, when this guy physically started abusing her. At the time of her death she was five months pregnant and had ended the relationship, accepting she would raise her child as a single mother. Unbeknown to her family, four months before her death she wrote in her diary: “I know I have messed up for twelve months and now I have to face the consequences of my actions. I am starting my life without you and writing that on its own, is “reliefing”. Today is the last day any man abuses me (mentally, emotionally, physically). I have bruises on my body and the smile on your face after hurting me, shows how sick you are. God, please send me a miracle.” THEMBA: About a month before her death I came home from work, I found her crying and she just volunteered the information that she had been assaulted by her boyfriend. He tried to strangle her right in the house. I asked him not to set his foot here again. He agreed and he left. But Themba says Thato continued threatening and contacting Zanele. A month later, he raped and strangled her at her parents house. BONGANI: How big a role does sexual jealousy play? LISA VETTEN: It is probably the leading precipitating factor. You are mine, and if you leave me, I am not going to be able to tolerate that kind of insult to my ego. LEONARD CARR: The key element that is a common dominator is that in the killing of another there is the objectification of the other – the other becomes merely an object of your gratification when that person no longer serves you or serves your interests, then it is more convenient to just get rid of them, dispose of them, you do that. Clinical psychologist, Leonard Carr even goes so far as to call intimate femicide a form of divorce. LEONARD CARR: It has become a highly practised form of divorce, because particularly in this country where there is so much hijacking, I have clients who are petrified because they know that their partners hare taken hits on them, so with hijacking it is certainly a way to dispose of someone without anybody being any wiser. Fatima Patel was murdered in April in her house in Polokwane. Her family is still in shock says her uncle, Farook Choonara. BONGANI: Did anyone in the family see this coming? FAROOK CHOOKARA: No, we all thought they were a happy couple. You know, we all want to find how did this… what happened, how did this thing take place. Fatima’s husband, Rameez was arrested less than a week after she died and released on bail of R250 000. He has not yet pleaded to the charge, but maintains he’s innocence, claiming robbers killed his wife. The case continues. FAROOK CHOONARA: The family want justice. Her skull was cracked, her cheekbones were broken, her jaw was dislodged, on top of all, she was still shot in her face. Anni says common themes run through most intimate femicide killings. ANNI: The motives here often are for financial reasons, adultery or a love-triangle and or whether there is a custody or a residential battle for children – Two hitmen were allegedly paid by Jayde Panayioutou’s husband, Christopher. Jayde was murdered after being kidnapped outside their house in Port Elizabeth in April. Her body was found on the outskirts of KwaNobuhle, outside Uitenhage. Panayioutou was arrested and charged with conspiracy to commit murder and defeating the ends of justice. He indicated he would plead not guilty. He was denied bail, but is appealing this ruling. Hitmen were also used to kill Chanelle Henning. Her parents, Sharon and Ivan believe a custody battle between their daughter and her estranged husband, Nico Henning was motive for her murder. Her two killers pleaded guilty and are serving 18-year sentences. Nico’s best friend, Andre Gouws and former Nigerian Olympic athlete, Ambrose Monye, confessed to being involved after they were convicted and are both serving life-sentences. Nico was arrested in December 2013 after Gouws testified he had offered him a million rand to have his wife killed. The trial starts on the 5th of October and he has not yet pleaded to the charges of murder and conspiracy to murder. BONGANI: Was it ever your sense that Nico could be a dangerous person? Ivan: Everything about him was just in place. He used to treat her well, he used to spoil her well, he used to respect us. BONGANI: How long did the good times last? Sharon: When they got back from honeymoon, she told us, that was the biggest mistake she made, because the day they got married, he changed and he was totally a different person. He became very abusive, not physically, but breaking her down every chance he got. LEONARD CARR: No abuser ever knocks on your door for a date and says: “Good evening, nice to meet you, do you want to enter into an abusive relationship with me?” Rather it starts out very charming and then the negative behaviour will be subtle, it will be a look, a remark, that makes the other person feel upset or put down. But then it will be followed by charm. So what you see is that abusers always switch BONGANI: Why did Chanelle stay? Sharon: Well, she didn’t. She tried to leave him a few times. She left him twice and he begged her everytime to come back LISA VETTEN: There may be threats that if you leave, I can’t live without you. And that might sound very flattering that someone loves you so much that they would rather die, but it is actually very dangerous. BONGANI LINK: The statistics around intimate femicide are truly shocking. This problem is a lot more prevalent than many of us are comfortable to believe. So, how are we all playing a part in aiding it? Most people avoid get involved in a neighbour’s or family member’s domestic disputes. LISA VETTEN: What has happened in people’s homes, is none of our business, we don’t get involved. They must sort it out between the two of them. BONGANI LINK: There is no doubt that the SA police service is under pressure to deal with very violent crimes. But how sensitized is the average officer to deal with intimate femicide? LISA VETTEN: Unfortunately, we know have for example four cases that have been brought against the police, two successful so far, two are still being heard, that have pointed to police negligence and the police had to pay damages. They had resulted in police failing to act on violence and resulted in women being raped or murdered. In 2009, 55 of the women who were killed in that year by their intimate partners, had protection orders at the time. THEMBA: Had I known the seriousness of the situation as a father, I would have done something. My daughter would be alive today had she had been open with us. SHARON: A year before she was murdered, we actually said to them at court, the legal team, if you guys do not do something now to protect her, he is going to have her killed and they told me in court that I am paranoid. Three weeks before she was murdered she asked us to promise her that if anything happens to her, we would fight for her son and that is what we did. Chanelle and Nico’s son was four when his mother was gunned down. He was placed in foster care for eight months after her death, while Ivan and Sharon fought for custody. Sharon: we had to undergo evaluations to make sure we are normal and can take care of him and that is something that I can’t get over, because you have lost your daughter, your grandson that has been living with you for 18 months gets ripped away from you, because of a system. Benjamin should have been with us, not with strangers. The custody battle is ongoing and Nico has unsupervised visits every second weekend. BONGANI LINK: At the core of public support for the court system, is not only the idea that justice is done, but that justice is seen to be done. This however, is threatened when people believe that perpetrators are given lenient sentences. Henning, Patel and Panayioutou will face their day in court. Kutumelo is currently serving a 20 year sentence and will remain behind bars for at least three-quarters of this term. THEMBA: I don’t know whether the sentences that the culprits are given in court are not deterrent enough. It is painful for us parents to have gone through this. FAROOK: If you have a problem with a person, why can’t you come to an amicable settlement, each one go their way, why do you have to murder a person? SHARON: It is time our system and our country take this kind of killing very serious, because this is not right. Our daughters and our grandchildren’s mothers shouldn’t be killed for any reason. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): SA holds the highest Femicide rate in the world - five times higher than the rate globally. They're almost always all beautiful and young, why are they being killed?
metadata.Summary: SA holds the highest Femicide rate in the world - five times higher than the rate globally. They're almost always all beautiful and young, why are they being killed? Intimate Femicide - the killing of a female by an intimate partner (husband, boyfriend, life partner) is considered to be the most extreme form and consequence of intimate partner violence. It is the leading cause of death for female murder victims in South Africa. A woman is killed by her intimate partner every eight hours in South Africa - three women a day. Globally, more than 35% of all murders of women are reported to be committed by an intimate partner.
metadata.Further information: In comparison, 5% of all murders on men are committed by an intimate partner. Evidence also shows that when women kill their intimate partners, it is mostly done in self-defence following ongoing violence and intimidation. When we hear of a women who was murdered, what jumps to mind first is whether her husband or boyfriend of life partner was involved. Why? In South Africa we have had a litany of high-profile cases that have been characterized in this way. The most obvious example is Oscar Pistorius shooting his model-girlfriend in the early hours of Valentine's Day in 2013 in his house in Pretoria. He was found guilty on culpable homicide, sentenced to five years in prison, and will be released on correctional supervision on 21 August this year after serving once sixth of his prison term. The NPA is appealing Judge Masipa's verdict in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein in November, asking that it be overturned to a guilty conviction on murder. Shrien Dewani, the so-called honeymoon murder accused, stood trial for arrnaging a hit on his wife, Anni in Gugulethu in November 2012. Three men were arrested in connection with the murder and they claimed Dewani offered them money to kill Anni, but he was aquitted. Nico Henning, allegedly the mastermind behind the killing of his estranged wife, Chanelle Henning in November 2011, will stand trial in October. Chanelle was gunned down in Faerie Glen just after dropping her son off at school. Tato Kutumela was convicted and sentenced ten years for raping and 20 years for killing his 18-year old model girlfriend, Zanele Khumalo in April 2011. He raped her, strangled her and covered her naked body with a blanket in her parents house in Pretoria, before he dressed and left for work. At the same time that Oscar Pistorius stood trial, Tato Kutumela was in the court next door was days in March last year, for proceedings in mitigation of his 20-year jail sentence. Dieter Bergs, 79, was charged in September last year for the murder of his wife of 10 years, Genee Bergs, national publicity manager of Estee Lauder. She was shot through the chest twice in March last year and at first Bergs claimed it was a robbery and that he had also injured his hip. Bergs is well-known in social circles in Johannesburg and had also served on the board of the Johannesburg Philharmonic Orchestra. He was arrested in September last years and released on bail of R10 000. Rameez Patel has been released on bail last month in Polokwane for the murder of his wife. At first Patel also claimed there was a burglary. Christopher Panayioytou has been denied bail and is being held in custody in Port Elizabeth for the alleged murder on his young wife, Jayde. She disappeared and a day later her body was found on the outskirts of Uitenhage in the Eastern Cape. A love triangle is being put forward by the state as a possible motive for the murder.
